answer_a:
Consistent tracking of internal heat is emphasized throughout the presentation, as culinary experts use on-screen digital overlays to monitor the progress of the roasting bird. In the preparation area with the yellow storage drawers and tiled walls, a blue graphic in the corner of the screen displays a measured value of 164 degrees while the individual gestures toward the appliance.

The specialist in the other cooking environment, which is marked by a small bonsai tree resting on the counter, clarifies how different muscle types respond to heat throughout the cycle. The active muscles found in the legs and wings are noted for their high fat content and dense collagen structure. The explanation highlights that a target of 175 degrees is the standard for these sections to ensure they render completely and achieve a tender consistency.

When the 164-degree reading is evaluated against the established criteria for active muscles, it represents a measurement that has yet to reach the target rendering state. Although this numeric value is near the safe zone for other parts of the bird, it remains separate from the 175-degree requirement needed for dark meat to reach its optimal texture through the rendering process.
answer_b:
Internal temperature tracking is a recurrent priority in the video, with the speakers using advanced digital displays to verify the readiness of the roasted poultry. In the kitchen area characterized by the large potted fern on the shelf, the individual holds a black electronic probe that captures a measurement of 164 degrees while the bird is being cooked in the workspace.

The expert positioned in the alternative preparation environment, which features multiple horizontal shelves filled with diverse literature, explains why hitting specific thermal marks is necessary for different anatomical parts. Because active muscles such as the legs and wings are composed of tougher connective tissue and fat, they require higher temperatures to reach a tender state. Reaching a level of 175 degrees is necessary to allow the collagen to render into a succulent and soft texture.

As the reading of 164 is compared to the standards explained for active muscles, it is evident that this state is still transitioning toward the required rendering point. While the 164-degree mark is sufficient for basic safety in white meat sections, it remains lower than the 175-degree threshold prescribed for the dark meat portions to reach their peak quality through fat rendering.
